report:
**Conclusion: yes—if “regularly” means repeated *low-dose* CT screening in people at sufficiently high risk.** The best evidence is randomized trials, and it shows fewer **lung-cancer deaths**, not that CT prevents cancer.

* In the U.S. NLST, high-risk current or former smokers assigned to three annual low-dose CT scans had about a **20% lower lung-cancer mortality** than those assigned to chest X-rays.  
  https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873

* The Dutch-Belgian NELSON randomized trial, comparing repeated volume-based low-dose CT with no screening in current/former smokers, likewise found significantly lower lung-cancer mortality (about **24% lower among men** at 10 years). This independent replication makes the result persuasive.  
  https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793

**Important qualifications:** the benefit was demonstrated in selected high-risk people and in organized screening programs with expert follow-up—not in everyone who has ever smoked, nor for a one-off conventional CT. A smaller Danish randomized trial did *not* find a statistically significant mortality reduction, plausibly in part because it was much smaller; that is evidence for uncertainty about the precise size of benefit, rather than strong evidence of no benefit.  
https://academic.oup.com/ajrccm/article/193/5/542/8508770

Screening also causes harm: false alarms, extra imaging and sometimes invasive procedures, radiation exposure, and overdiagnosis (finding cancers that would not have caused illness). The USPSTF estimates that in NLST, per 1,000 screened, false-positive findings led to 17 invasive procedures. Thus the decision should be individualized and paired with smoking-cessation support.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/evidence-summary14/lung-cancer-screening
